#345. Roli Has Fallen Apart—and Left Customers Holding the Bag

Roli, the company behind expressive, touch-sensitive music devices like the Seaboard and Roli Blocks, has collapsed.

Although it hasn't been officially announced, Roli reportedly ousted its CEO and founder, Roland Lamb, earlier this year. Since then, Roli has all but dissolved. (In August, a new company called Instrumental Intelligence was registered with the UK government under Lamb's name, a potential move by the founder to acquire Roli's assets).

On Monday, Roli emailed users that two licensed insolvency practitioners were appointed joint administrators of Roli on October 20. The company went into administration, the UK process that manages corporate insolvency. This is the second time Roli has gone bankrupt.

That has left a small but bereft community of customers with no word on getting the products they paid for. The Roli community has expressed sadness, anger, or outright confusion. In Facebook groups, the r/Roli subreddit, and other forums, dismayed users have struggled to find recourse for Roli equipment purchases ranging from hundreds to thousands of dollars. The Roli subreddit has been awash with posts from customers who say they paid for orders months or years ago and have received no response or refund since then.

Existing owners also worry about the long-term impact. Roli instruments rely heavily on proprietary software launchers and companion apps to connect, map sounds, and configure settings. While the hardware still functions, users fear that lack of software support will eventually leave their gear bricked.

Roli has not publicly communicated about its future strategy with customers. The company did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment; Lamb did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Roli’s primary financial backers, investment firms TriplePoint Capital and Hoxton Ventures, also did not respond.

Roli has faced financial struggles before.

The company started in 2009 but really took off after musician Pharrell Williams invested in 2017 and Sony’s Innovation Fund in 2018. Musicians like Dream Theater keyboardist Jordan Rudess supported and touted Roli’s gadgets. Ryan Gosling’s character played a Seaboard Grand in the 2016 movie La La Land. In the late 2010s, the tech and the company were hailed as a hit.

That tune changed in 2020. The British government’s Future Fund—a taxpayer-funded relief package issued to help businesses during the pandemic—partially bailed out Roli from a Covid-19-induced financial crisis. Even then, Roli went into administration for the first time in 2021. It survived by relaunching as Luminary Roli and focusing on music-learning devices like the light-up Lumi keyboard and the Airwave, a digital theremin that doubled as an AI piano teacher.

Through all of that, customers have had issues with how the company communicates. Users who ordered the Lumi keyboard found orders unexpectedly delayed, with no indication from the company on what was happening.

“One of the problems they have had ever since I started with the Kickstarter is communication and explaining things—telling people what's going on,” Lluís Gerard, a YouTuber who has reviewed Roli products for years under the handle WasabiNoise, tells WIRED. “There's always been too much secrecy about things, or then you'd realize, oh, there are these delays.”

Former Roli employees—who spoke with WIRED but asked not to be named to avoid jeopardizing future employment opportunities—alleged a company culture that revolved around Lamb’s whims. Every person we spoke with who worked with Lamb compared him to a Steve Jobs-esque character. One person described the experience of being at Roli as being in a movie, where Lamb saw himself as the main character and everyone else as extras or set pieces.

“I love the company, love the culture, love the people—I didn’t love working for him,” the employee said. “Everyone has their story with him. You're buckled into his car—and he’s not going in the right direction.”

In 2021, another former Roli employee, who also asked not to be identified, uploaded files on GitHub that include various notes chronicling Roli as a hostile workplace. One 16-page PDF is titled “Keeping Roland Happy” and includes multiple sections about how to handle interacting with a pathological narcissist. Several former employees independently described what they viewed as Lamb’s narcissistic behavior, describing him as an arrogant visionary.

“Roland is the archetype of a pathological narcissist,” one employee told WIRED. “Unfortunately, that's what he became. Incredibly brittle when challenged, absolutely shameless, quite reckless, incapable of learning or growth, would rather gamble than take any lessons from the previous experience. It was very disheartening to see.”

“The tragedy here is that it was always fundamentally a great company,” another former employee says. “A lot of what made it great was the sort of all-powerful vision of the founder. But that was so obviously the critical flaw.”

Along with other touch-sensitive devices like the Linnstrument and the Sensel Morph, Roli was a key company in the rise of MIDI polyphonic expression (MPE) devices. MPE technology lets players control a note’s pitch and timbre through touch-based movement. Pressing or sliding fingers over the device’s surface produces varying MIDI notes that capture more expressive playing.

While inventive, Roli’s instruments were altogether very niche—a hard product category to build an Apple-sized audience around. Roli certainly tried, partnering with Apple to sell its Roli Blocks in Apple Stores. Alas, the pandemic caused dire supply chain issues, and the company couldn’t keep up with orders. After the pandemic, bankruptcy, and the rebrand, little remained to push the company forward except the founder's will.

“This was one of the leading lights of music technology in the world,” one former employee said. “It was truly an inventing company—the stuff it made had never been made before. So it's a real shame.”

The response to Roli’s collapse hasn’t been pure dismay. After months of delays and frustration, Reddit users have gathered to mourn the company—and to make sure its devices keep working.

Sam Hocking, a UK audio engineer who runs an audio tools company called Demix.me, also owns multiple Roli Seaboard Blocks. Even before Roli went into administration, Hocking had been building software that could keep the equipment working as a capable MIDI device. He shared his vibe-coded configuration tools in the Roli subreddit and on GitHub, so Roli’s Grand, Rise, Airwave, and Block devices can work without the Roli launcher.

Hocking says his Seaboards are nearly 10 years old and still working. Despite the company’s rocky history and poor communication, he still wants to keep his devices. They’re high quality, cost a good chunk of money, and feel somewhat irreplaceable.

He’s not alone. Other users on the subreddit have joined in, adding their own tweaks and fixes to the software that may keep at least a few of these devices alive.

“They're quite a unique product; there's not another keyboard type out there,” Hocking says. “Nobody likes to spend money and then not be able to use it.”

#344. Black Friday vs. Cyber Monday: Which day should you shop for the best deals?

Once two distinct deal shopping days, Black Friday and Cyber Monday have basically merged into one massive shopping extravaganza. The lines really began to blur when the world shut down in 2020 and brick-and-mortar stores hosted online sales in lieu of in-person Black Friday events. In 2026, lines outside stores are practically nonexistent. We certainly can't see them.

While major retailers will be running holiday sales throughout all of November, savvy shoppers know that Black Friday, Cyber Monday, (and the few days surrounding them) still remain the absolute biggest shopping days of the year for their ability to reliably trigger record-low prices on big-ticket items (like TVs, Apple devices, smartwatches, headphones, and of course, Amazon's own devices). That includes discounts that beat Amazon's massively-hyped October Prime Day deals.

If you're debating when you should start adding big ticket items to your cart and whether it's better to shop on Black Friday or Cyber Monday, you've come to the right place. After years of covering both sales extensively, here's our expert analysis.

Way back in the age of MySpace and AIM — aka 2005 — the National Retail Federation debuted the term "Cyber Monday" after realizing that the Monday after Thanksgiving saw a flood of online sales. This was likely due to shoppers using their faster internet connections at work on Monday morning to snag deals, or at least that's what they credited it to. That, of course, and the fact that online retailers wanted some of that holiday shopping bread, too. Thus, two distinct deal shopping days were born: Black Friday, for those who wanted to shop in stores the day after Thanksgiving, and Cyber Monday, for those who liked shopping from the comfort of their desks.

Over 20 years later, there's little — if any — real difference between the two due to the alleged "death of retail." Everyone and everything is online, so why wouldn't Black Friday be? Based on our years of experience covering both, we can truly say neither is a "better" day to shop. It really comes down to what you're looking for and how much demand there is for it. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

If you see a solid deal, grab it, no matter which sale title it falls under. There's not a tremendous amount of distinction anymore in terms of discounts on particular products as there has been in previous years. However, there are still rules to follow in some product categories: TV deals tend to be more dramatic and widespread for Black Friday with a higher likelihood of selling out before the clock even turns to Cyber Monday, while waiting for Cyber Monday to double-check that there's not a new, better laptop deal is often wise.

But with the blurred lines of Cyber Week, many of these deals will cross over. As noted at BlackFriday.com, "Some TV deals will feature flashy discounts during Black Friday and Cyber Monday, but they might not have the specs you're after." TL;DR: The deals will be great for both shopping days, but it all depends on what you're looking for. If you see the specs you like listed under a product sitting at a price that you like, grab it to be safe. Also, as a best practice, check camelcamelcamel.com for price history details from Amazon.

Black Friday proper falls on Nov. 27 in 2026, but it's honestly silly at this point to even call it Black Friday. It's no longer just on Friday — it's a month-long affair. You can shop deals at practically every retailer starting right after Halloween (before, even), with most labeling something an "early Black Friday deal" starting in early November. Best Buy has announced the official early deals of its Black Friday sale will begin Nov. 6, while Target's first early Black Friday sale kicks off on Nov. 5. In other words, if you want to get some early shopping done, have at it.

Once the clock strikes midnight at the close of Friday, it's basically Cyber Monday (yes, even though it's actually Saturday). We don't make the rules. The deals won't change too much, but the search terms and official site banners will.

Officially, Cyber Monday is on Monday, Nov. 30 in 2026. Unofficially, it basically starts the second Black Friday ends, with retailers coining sales as "Cyber Monday" deals as early as Saturday, Nov. 28. So basically, semantics — and it's easier to just think of the Cyber Week language as interchangeable.

Black Friday will last most of November, but come Saturday, Nov. 28, it's Cyber Monday time. As we mentioned above, since Black Friday and Cyber Monday are basically one massive shopping holiday, you likely won't see that many changes in deals, just changes in the banners and advertising of them.

Cyber Monday sales will last from Saturday, Nov. 28 to midnight on Monday, Nov. 30. There's not a hard stop, as there's always deals that stay live for at least the day or two following, but the large bulk of the sale is over once Monday ends.

As store policy, Target stores are closed on Thanksgiving Day, but are open for Black Friday beginning at 6 a.m. local time on Friday, Nov. 27.

Walmart will be open from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. local time on Friday, Nov. 27. Walmart has confirmed that physical stores will be closed on Thanksgiving Day "so associates can spend the day with their families."

All physical Best Buy locations will be closed on Thanksgiving. Doors will open at 6 a.m. local time on Friday, Nov. 27 for shoppers and close at 10 p.m.

All Kohl's stores are closed on Thanksgiving but are open for in-store shopping beginning at 5 a.m. local time on Nov. 27, per a press release.

#343. Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships

Why rationing agentic coding backfires, and what to measure instead.

When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive.

The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028.

The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap.

A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality.

If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces.

Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work.

Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself.

A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload.

Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work.

Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows.

The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request.

Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting.

At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. The result: token costs down 30 to 50%.

That is the point of hybrid. With HPE Private Cloud AI, owning your inference does not mean giving up frontier models. Run the volume on capacity you own and let a gateway send the hardest work.

Data also shows that usage, not licensed headcount, drives spend. The top 5% of users generated most of the consumption, and the heaviest used roughly 450 times more than the lightest on the same license. If power users grow from a small minority to half the workforce, monthly spend can rise about 4.4 times with flat headcount. Your mix will differ, which is exactly why you need to measure it.

HPE tracks two metrics and recommends customers do the same. First, it tracks cost per active developer, because averaging across all licenses hides the power users driving spend. Second, it tracks cost per merged pull request, because it connects AI spending to software that ships.

Baseline both costs before changing infrastructure. Then run a complete development cycle on owned capacity. If both metrics do not improve as usage grows, your current model may still be the better choice.

Owned capacity is not for everyone. Low or unpredictable usage favors APIs, with no capital tied up in idle infrastructure. Ownership pays off when sustained demand keeps it busy. Most enterprises will run hybrid: frontier APIs for demanding or intermittent work, owned capacity for repeatable volume. A governed gateway decides what leaves the building, so you get frontier models without giving up sovereignty over your code.

As developers lean harder on coding agents, usage will keep rising. The real choice is whether that growth shows up as a bigger variable-cost bill or as more software shipped on capacity you own. The companies that lead AI-assisted development will not ration adoption to control costs. They will build an operating model where more AI use improves the economics instead of undermining them.

Apple robot backed by CEO John Ternus may have hefty price tag and limited uses.

Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room.

People who worked on Apple’s robotic projects told The Information that the AI-driven home robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra in line with Apple’s new HomeView stationary smart display. The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028.

The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project. The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies.

However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households. Is there a market for a smart home device costing more than $1,000 that moves around while hosting FaceTime calls, automatically handling room lights, and occasionally ordering the family cat to get off the dining table?

One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years. The software side boasts a significantly larger team of approximately 300 people.

Still, Ternus has been backing this home robot as well as a separate Apple project focused on developing robots for household tasks like folding clothes, according to The Information. The latter would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, though it’s unclear if that means Apple has ambitions to develop a general-purpose humanoid robot for household use like robotics startups 1X and Figure AI.

From a technical and safety standpoint, Apple’s initial focus on a limited-purpose home robot still makes much more sense right now than any attempt to develop a general-purpose autonomous robot that could pose greater risks when operating near humans. The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.

#341. Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics

The top reason analytics agents produce substandard insights is a lack of business context, prompting investment in semantic layers and governance, rather than bigger models.

In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired.

Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed.

Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business.

Some key findings from the report include the following:

Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses.

Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights.

Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context.

Insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness. At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon. Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive.

Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights. The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%). They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%). The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents.

#339. Here’s Why You Shouldn’t Use AI to Vote

As Americans go to the polls today, many will have had their decision about who to vote for informed by an artificial intelligence–powered chatbot.

Around 50 percent of recently surveyed US adults have at one time used an AI chatbot, and 8 percent say they have used these tools ahead of the midterms to find information on candidates and policies, according to Pew Research.

But a lot of information from these chatbots is out of date and has been hallucinated or sourced from partisan websites.

Even supposedly nonpartisan chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini have been found wanting when it comes to questions about the midterms.

Just last week, Google’s AI Mode refused to provide the results of the 2020 elections, and the company’s Gemini chatbot said the deadline to request a mail-in ballot in Pennsylvania was November 3, rather than the real deadline of October 27, according to research by Forum AI.

According to the Forum AI research, almost 40 percent of election answers given by all the mainstream chatbots contained at least one factual error. In August, when Forum AI’s researchers asked why someone should vote for North Carolina congressman Don Davis, Claude gave a response that conflated the lawmaker with a “former school superintendent” of the same name.

Google and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment. Open AI directed WIRED to a blog outlining the company’s approach to elections in 2026.

Part of the problem is that chatbots are reliant on an increasingly problematic pool of online information. Research by NewsGuard found that mainstream chatbots cite so-called “pink slime” websites nearly 50 percent of the time when asked about candidates and policies related to the midterms. Pink slime sites present as mainstream news websites but are in fact funded by political or ideological groups and individuals.

Ahead of the midterms, many more of these sites have sprung up, and chatbots are paying attention. The worst offender, according to NewsGuard, was OpenAI’s ChatGPT, which cited the pink slime sites in more than 70 percent of searches, while xAI’s Grok chatbot performed best, citing pink slime sites in 30 percent of cases.

“I don't think that most Americans are prepared to navigate an election in the age of consumer AI,” Nina Jankowicz, executive director of the American Sunlight Project and a former disinformation czar during the Biden administration, tells WIRED. “One of the problems is that executives and companies have really overpromised on what AI is capable of. It has to ingest this information from somewhere, and often those sources are not very good. And it's predictive, so if it doesn't know the answer, it does frequently make things up.”

#338. Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test

One month into the attempted rebrand of “AI,” the term is not catching on. But it’s sure to muddy our national conversation about AI anyway.

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.

Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).

The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government.

It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the new term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”).

But most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada. AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week. It might be the boldest rebrand yet.

Let’s start with the government itself. The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a new request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities. The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites. Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period.

There have been hiccups. A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon announced an ambitious new initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology. A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language.

The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order says it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents).

As for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue. One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up. Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3.

But Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary. It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too.

In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms. But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a new rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents.

But the Wall Street Journal is not alone: Even Newsmax, an outlet whose founder described it as “supportive of the President and his policies,” isn’t using the president’s preferred term.

Are Big Tech executives falling in line? It’s complicated. The same day that President Trump signed the rebranding order, he also released a nonbinding statement on AI safety, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six of the most powerful people in tech: Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia.

But even among this group—three members of which attended Trump’s inauguration—the term has not caught on.

In an analysis of third-quarter earnings calls, CNBC reported that only Zuckerberg and Musk used the term consistently. But Zuckerberg doesn’t quite count: Meta has been saying “superintelligence” since last year anyway. Musk’s companies seem to use the term the most—and he even pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Musk himself still mixes SI and AI when posting on X.

Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet used “AI” in their calls, though Microsoft’s recent letter to shareholders referred to the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but still uses AI too.

One objection to this rebranding project is that it will cost time and taxpayer dollars. It is Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff’s prerogative to decide that SIForce is a better name than AIForce and direct his company to implement that change. But government employees are now spending time writing guides on how departments should navigate the rebrand. And, per the executive order, leaders of federal agencies will be required to put their heads together to draft a new legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” to be run by the president by the end of this month.

But I’m more worried about what this does to our national conversation about AI than I am about the potential waste of time and money. Surprisingly often I overhear strangers at a grocery store or coffee shop who have struck up a conversation about AI. The substance of the conversation is rarely uplifting—they most often talk about a jobs apocalypse or AI-powered warfare—but what is heartening is how often I see a widespread desire among people to have a say in how this technology transforms their lives.

People may have wildly different feelings about AI, including outright hostility, but those differences don’t yet map neatly onto the partisan divisions that make it awkward for strangers to discuss immigration or climate change.

If “Super Intelligence” turns into a loyalty test, this will cease to be the case. It’s easy to imagine that two people chatting about, say, whether chatbots are good or bad for our mental health will stop once they realize one of them is saying “super intelligence” and the other “AI.” That would be a shame for us all.

Midterm elections are tomorrow. Americans say AI is more important to them in this election than environmental and climate policy (and Democrats even rank it above abortion and gun policy). We’re only just beginning to have a national conversation about what AI will mean for our lives. Whether or not “Super Intelligence” catches on, turning the terminology itself into a loyalty test will do nothing to advance a national conversation about AI that’s only just getting started.

#335. Most of our measures of a key cognitive process don't agree

A big study with very little beyond negative results still gets published.

It’s widely acknowledged that it’s nearly impossible to publish negative results in scientific journals. “We didn’t see anything” is a much harder sell than finding that a hypothesis is clearly right. Findings of no effect tend to either be shuffled off to low-profile journals or left behind as unpublished lab lore.

The high-profile journal Nature, however, made a notable exception this week, publishing a study that tells us that a bunch of methods we have been using to try to measure a key emotional ability don’t seem to be measuring the same thing. The results mean that we don’t have a good way to measure the impact of a concept that is the basis of a key method in therapy.

One of the most successful forms of therapy is cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT. In part, CBT is based on getting people to step back and engage in “cognitive reappraisal.” This requires people to think over a situation that has caused a negative emotional response and find ways to reinterpret it so that it has less impact on them. The ability to engage in this process has been linked to emotional resilience.

Given its importance, a lot of studies have looked at what’s going on in the brain when people engage in cognitive reappraisal. There are also a number of questionnaires that are thought to measure a person’s capacity to engage in the process. So, a large international collaboration of researchers decided to look at these more carefully. “We focused on three widely used indices that are often assumed to reflect related facets of reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings following reappraisal, and amygdala down-regulation during reappraisal,” they wrote.

The amygdala is a structure deep in the brain that tends to be active when people have emotional responses to events (as well as in a wide variety of additional circumstances). So, it makes sense to expect that it would be less active if people were trying to tone down their emotions. But to find out whether that’s actually correct, you need to look at brain activity. Here, the team relied on 40 functional MRI data sets, providing a large enough data set to tease out even relatively small effects.

Which is a good thing, because the effects really were hard to detect. “The effect size was comparatively small: To detect this effect size with a statistical power of 80 percent, a single study would need to test 1,105 participants,” the researchers note, going on to say that very few fMRI studies have access to anywhere near that many subjects.

But there were even bigger problems when the differences among individuals in the MRI data were compared to their differences in the questionnaires or task-based ratings. Almost none of the variance in the different measures correlated with each other. We could go through the numbers, but a figure from the paper makes the issue quite clear.

Further issues became apparent when the researchers started looking at activity in the areas of the brain that are responsible for high-level decision-making. If people were really engaging their ability to re-evaluate emotional triggers, presumably these areas should be active, as they are needed to power the re-evaluation process.

But that wasn’t what the fMRI data showed. Instead, there was a correlation between the response of the amygdala and the response elsewhere in the brain. In other words, if the amygdala was very active, implying a stronger emotional response, then activity in the decision-making areas of the brain was also higher. If the emotional response seemed tamped down, then activity in the reasoning centers was lower as well.

In a bit of an understatement, the researchers declared, “These findings call for a fundamental reassessment of how reappraisal capacity is measured and interpreted across behavioural and neural levels of analysis.”

The primary issue is that these three ways of looking at emotional regulation were thought to be exploring the same thing, but it’s clear that they’re not. As the researchers point out, this probably shouldn’t be viewed as a surprise. The questionnaires typically ask about overall personality tendencies, and so cover a very long time period. The answers are also likely to implicate a variety of traits beyond simple emotional control.

Both the task-based ratings and fMRI work, by contrast, capture in-the-moment responses. But they do so under very, very different experimental circumstances—namely, one of them involves being stuffed in an MRI tube. Beyond that, many of the fMRI experiments involve simplifying the process of emotional regulation in order to get consistent data. It’s entirely possible that these differences also influence brain activity in a variety of ways.

So, the take-home appears to be that re-evaluation of emotional responses may be a real phenomenon, but we don’t currently have tools that can clearly capture the process effectively. Gaining that ability may require developing new methods, and thinking more clearly about what different stages of the re-evaluation process require. In the meantime, the people behind this work caution that “strong claims about a person’s emotion regulation capacity based on any specific brain region should be made with considerable caution.”

Nature, 2025. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11203-1  (About DOIs).

#334. How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check

Borrowing from disciplines like economics could help AI safety researchers control AI models, even if they don’t understand them.

A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.

Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution—a sort of moral code.

The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions, and mislead their evaluators.

Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage.

An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay.

In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.

A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).

Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.

The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.

A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?”

Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.

During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.

There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.

Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.

Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.”

One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.

It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.

“Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior.

Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. Models could find loopholes that no one anticipated. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.)

Whatever these mechanisms look like, they will ultimately have to slot into the biggest mechanism of all: the free market. “We play by the rules of economics,” says Hazan. A more aligned model may be good for the world, but if it’s slower or more expensive than a less aligned one, does our current system of rules and regulations actually incentivize any of the frontier labs to release it?

“It’s a mechanism that’s responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind,” he says of the market, “but it could be ultimately responsible for something very terrible.” Perhaps the entities really in need of a better mechanism design are the labs themselves.

#333. LA communities kick out Big Oil

After years of advocacy from residents and legal battles with Big Oil, Los Angeles voted to ban drilling and phase out oil extraction in the city. It's the first city in the United States to kick the oil industry out.

Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .

"Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," said local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells. Existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.

Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

"In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," said council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site."

Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property."

LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.

California's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

Today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.

Under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," said Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.

Miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.

LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.

California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman said energy companies were prepared to challenge the new ordinance.

Zierman added that it would make city residents more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.

"It sends the jobs, investment and revenue elsewhere while leaving Californians to pay the bill," said Zierman.

The relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

Even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

California's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the coastal lowlands known as the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.

When wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA fire department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.

But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

The cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging plans or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.

But those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million (€32 million) in fines in 2025.

A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup."  For now, she is says both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air."

A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal.

Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice.

#331. Binance Says Hackers Used Well-Known Tricks to Carry Out a $6.34 Billion Heist

For almost a decade, North Korean cybercriminals have targeted the cryptocurrency industry—large and small. While these hacks have been frequent, the country’s hackers allegedly made off with their biggest heist to date last week when $6.34 billion was siphoned from the wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.

In a new security update issued on Tuesday, Binance detailed its initial findings into how the company was compromised and hackers were able to steal billions in just 20 minutes. The hack, according to Binance, was the result of an engineer falling for a fake job interview and downloading malicious software. The hackers were then able to move through the company’s network, exploit an internal AI tool, and gain access to a wallet signing service that allowed them to make transactions outside of normal withdrawal procedures.

“This should not have happened, and we apologize for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance wrote in its security update, where it also says it has set aside funds to cover the losses and has “rebuilt or replaced” internal systems impacted in the attack. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” the company says.

Although more than $6 billion was stolen from Binance accounts, almost half of this—where it was possible to do so—was frozen by parts of the cryptocurrency industry, meaning the hackers could not access the funds. However, that still leaves billions controlled by North Korea’s hackers, who have been trying to launder the stolen money into a form where it can be accessed and cashed out. That process could take months.

Binance’s analysis says the hack was the accumulation of months of work by hackers, with the ultimate attack taking place on October 29. Shortly after funds started to be moved from Binance’s hot wallets, across more than 10 different blockchains, multiple cryptocurrency tracing firms attributed the attacks to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) hackers, in particular the sophisticated TraderTraitor group that previously stole more than $1.5 billion in a separate hack last year. The FBI quickly linked TraderTraitor to the Binance hack on October 31.

“Binance’s account aligns with what we know about the TraderTraitor playbook,” says Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos. “The attackers didn’t simply steal a wallet key. They compromised engineers, used that access to understand and move through the environment, and ultimately subverted the systems used to authorize transactions.”

Binance stops short of directly blaming the TraderTraitor hackers itself; however, the company points to the FBI’s attribution to North Korea and acknowledges a prior targeting by DPRK’s cybercriminals. “Throughout 2026, Binance's security team detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases,” the company’s update says.

Binance says activity linked to the hack can first be traced back to June this year. At the time, its update says, an engineer the company refers to as Engineer A downloaded a “tampered Homebrew installation” they found searching online. While the company says this was detected and dealt with, information about the employee was later “exposed to the hacker.”

At the start of September, Binance says another software engineer, identified only as Engineer B, was contacted on “a legitimate job-hunting platform” and then attended a video interview where the fake recruiter shared legitimate-looking social media accounts and personal photos to make them seem real. The Binance engineer progressed, unsurprisingly, to a second-round interview that was conducted using an online chat. “Near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” Binance’s report says.

“The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server,” the company writes. It adds that hackers took steps to hide their activity, a common practice.

Toward the end of October, a little more than a week before the hack, Binance says, the attackers used their access to the engineer’s machine to “gain control” over the wallet of Engineer A, who had been compromised months earlier, and “another Wallet Software Engineer C.” Then on October 29, Binance says, the attackers logged in to the computer of another staff member, Software Engineer C, and used stolen login details before launching the attack. On the evening of the theft, according to Binance, the attack unfolded quickly. “The attacker exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to initiate transactions outside the normal withdrawal process,” the company writes.

Sophos’s Pilling says TraderTraitor “excels” in its attacks through detailed planning and being able to understand how the services of those it hacks operate. “The initial compromise is just a foothold,” he says. “The real attack is carefully engineered around how the victim actually moves money.”

While Binance says its findings are only the initial step of its investigation, security and crypto tracing experts say that the hackers are undertaking efforts to launder and cash out the stolen cryptocurrency. Since the start of 2017, according to analysis by TRM Labs, North Korean–linked hackers have stolen around $12 billion in cryptocurrency—with more than half of that coming from heists this year.

Despite the astronomical sums, it is unclear how much of this money makes it back to North Korea. As in the Binance case, some cryptocurrencies can be frozen and made inaccessible, while other transactions can be blocked by some cryptocurrency exchanges. Crypto tracing company Elliptic has said the laundering from the Binance attack has been “highly complex” and likely to be automated. “In its first three and a half days it used about 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains, roughly one new wallet every 25 seconds, and more than 40,000 transactions,” Elliptic cofounder and chief scientist Tom Robinson wrote in a blog post.

If the money can be laundered successfully, there is a chance it will be converted to cash and used to bolster the development of North Korea’s nuclear weapons program and ballistic missile systems, according to a report published last year from the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, which includes experts from the United States, South Korea, and nine other countries. “They are highly reliant on Chinese underground banking and China-based facilitators, though they sometimes rely upon facilitators in other countries.”

Shania Twain is standing up for others in country music.

#326. Googling "Zelda" today offers a glimpse of how search worked in 1998

The year was 1998. Britney Spears topped the charts, Bill Clinton was impeached, and a couple of little websites called Google and Ars Technica came online. It was also the year Nintendo released The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo 64. Google, which has come to dominate the Internet (Ars is still working on that), is celebrating the imminent release of the Ocarina of Time remaster by temporarily transporting us back to that storied year with a search Easter egg.

To access the Google time machine, you just have to search for either “Zelda” or “Ocarina of Time.” Google will load the standard 2026 results page, but you’ll see an animated Master Sword in the lower right corner. It appears on both mobile and desktop—just click the sword and enjoy the show.

After a little time-skipping animation and a Link shout (you know the one), you’ll swear it’s 1998 again. The search page is transformed into a simple list of blue links with retro Google branding. This is particularly apt given the time-shifting mechanics in Ocarina of Time.

Classic Google used to provide a list of 10 links on each page, but there are only seven included in the Easter egg. This is a curated list of links rather than a real search. You get the official Nintendo Zelda page, Zelda on Wikipedia, Zelda games on Amazon, and a couple more.

You can go back to the modern version of Google’s search results at any time by clicking the sword again. Oh, you don’t want to do that? Sadly, this is a very limited experience. The Google of today is much different, and if you try to search for anything from the retro interface, you are immediately booted back to 2026 with all the AI, sponsored content, suggested searches, and social media links.

The Ocarina of Time left its mark on a generation of gamers, and clearly, some of them went on to work at Google. The company’s intention is probably to leverage nostalgia to build hype for Nintendo’s big launch, but there’s also something a little sad about this. Google’s push into generative AI is transforming search in a way that many people don’t like. Seeing the simple, minimalist roots of Google search on display drives home how much the company’s core product has changed.

The Ocarina of Time has changed a lot, too. The remastered game has been completely re-created, with slick Switch 2 graphics, modern controls for movement and camera, numerous quality-of-life improvements, and more. The game is available for preorder now at $60 for digital and $70 for physical. It launches on November 5 for Nintendo Switch 2.

#325. NASA's Swift observatory is expected to return to Earth on November 4

The agency’s attempt to rescue it a few months ago had failed.

NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will re-enter our atmosphere around 3:30AM Eastern time tomorrow, November 4, according to the US Armed Forces' predictions. The exact time could be different, as the prediction has an "uncertainty of 11 hours." But the 3,200-pound spacecraft is heading back to Earth for sure, 22 years after it launched and after the agency's attempt to save it failed.

In early July, NASA launched the Swift Boost mission to rescue the space telescope, whose orbit was decaying too fast, in hopes that it could still gather data for the agency over the next few years. The mission was supposed to use Katalyst Space's LINK robotic spacecraft to dock with the observatory and then tug it back to a higher orbit. Unfortunately, LINK ran into attitude control issues that prevented it from controlling its orientation in space. As a result, the spacecraft kept on spinning helplessly, which also caused communication issues. A couple of weeks after LINK ran into problems, NASA had decided to pull the plug on the mission.

The agency ended Swift observatory's operations in late October after it entered safe mode and prepared for re-entry. Before its operations ended, though, Swift, had observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, or the most powerful explosions in the universe that reach peak brightness in less than two seconds. Before Swift, we couldn't detect these swift flashes of energy in time. It also gathered data on 1,400 supernova explosions, asteroids, comets, stars shredded by black holes, as well as other activity in the cosmos.

NASA says most of Swift will burn up in the atmosphere, but some components might survive and make its way to the ground. Don't worry, though: There's very little risk of any surviving fragment harming anyone. The agency and the Armed Forces are monitoring the falling telescope and will update predictions as needed.

#324. You can easily update your AirPods firmware in just a few simple steps

AirPods firmware updates can bring new features and improvements, but installing them is a bit obtuse.

Similar to how your iPhone gets regular software updates, AirPods sometimes receive firmware updates. At times, these updates simply improve reliability and fix bugs, but some also introduce new features. For example, some AirPods models gained a Custom EQ feature with the iOS 27 update. But you may have never heard of AirPods firmware updates since Apple hides this process from view.

It's not like updating iOS, where there's a dedicated page inside Settings to check for updates — everything happens silently in the background. The good news is that there are a few ways to trigger AirPods firmware updates, plus ways to check which version your earbuds are running.

Before updating your AirPods, you need to make sure you have an iPhone, iPad or Mac running the latest software. That's because new AirPods firmware updates often require the latest version of iOS or macOS. This is as simple as opening the Settings app, going to General and then choosing Software Update. If an update is available, you'll find it there. If not, your device will say you're running the latest version.

Now it's time to check which firmware version your AirPods are currently running. On an iPhone or iPad, connect your earbuds and open Settings — you'll see an AirPods menu at the top. Tap and scroll down until you find Version in the About section. On a Mac, open System Settings and go to the Bluetooth menu. Find your AirPods and click the i button on the right to find the same information.

Apple has an AirPods firmware page where you can check the latest version available for each model, so compare this to what you found to see if there's a newer release available. If the number doesn't match, your AirPods probably need a firmware update.

Now comes the tricky part. There's no way to directly force AirPods to install a new firmware update, and Apple says that firmware updates are "delivered automatically." However, the company does explain how to best prepare your earbuds for an update. First, make sure your AirPods are paired with your iPhone, iPad or Mac, and that the connected device has Bluetooth on. Your device also must be connected to Wi-Fi, because the update won't download over 4G or 5G.

Once everything looks good, put your AirPods in the charging case and plug it into a power source with the lid closed. Keep the earbuds within range of your device and wait about 30 minutes. After that, reconnect your AirPods and check the firmware version again.

The process is pretty much the same for AirPods Max — just put them in the case and plug them into a charger. If for some reason you use AirPods but don't have an Apple device, take your AirPods to an Apple Store or an Apple Authorized Service Provider, and they'll update the firmware for you.

Most new AirPods features are added through firmware updates, and sometimes these updates are major. Features such as Live Translation, studio-quality audio recording and remote camera control were all introduced with firmware updates for AirPods. Although new features are often exclusive to the latest models, even older models may still benefit from updates. Custom EQ, for example, works with all AirPods that have an H2 chip.

Of course, not every AirPods firmware update brings new features. Many of them are limited to the standard "bug fixes and other improvements" release notes. Still, these firmware updates can fix connection issues and other annoyances you might encounter while using AirPods, so it's always a good idea to keep them updated.

#323. Ice hockey officials considering options after CAS order to reinstate Russia

Ice hockey's ruling body is deciding how to respond to a decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport that allows Russia back into international competition. Germany hasn't ruled out pulling out as a tournament host.

The president of the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), Franz Reindl, announced shortly after the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday, that he had called a meeting of its main decision-making body for Monday and Tuesday.

The Lausanne-based court had ruled that the IIHF must allow Russian national teams to take part in ice hockey world championships again. They had been barred from doing so since shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"Our task now is to implement this ruling responsibly," said Germany's Reindl, who was elected IIHF president just last month.

"Several championships are only weeks away, and changes to participation affect many people; players, teams, organizing committees and host cities," he said. "We will work closely with all of them to find practical solutions."

The first tournament the CAS decision applies to is the World Juniors, to be held beginning on December 26 in Canada. Just how it will affect the tournament is not clear. Hockey Canada said it was in contact with the IIHF and had briefed Prime Minister Mark Carney's government on the decision.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand told public broadcaster CBC that she is "not comfortable" with allowing a Russian team to take part in the tournament in Alberta.

"This is a very unwelcome decision given the geopolitical situation, given the actions of Russia," she said. "All options are on the table, and I will say, again, I greet this decision with great disappointment."

Canada's secretary of state for sport, Adam van Koeverden, appeared to rule out Russian athletes being granted visas for the tournament

"Canada will maintain restrictions on the participation of Russian athletes at events hosted in Canada that receive funding from the Government of Canada and explore further options to ensure that the Russian government is held accountable," he said in a statement.

Germany is also considering its options as it prepares to host the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Düsseldorf and Mannheim in May.

"The German government takes a very critical view of the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, a government spokesman said on Sunday, according to the DPA news agency.

"The German government will discuss possible consequences of the ruling, including for the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany, with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) promptly."

The DEB's chief executive, Frank Lutz, is to travel to Berlin to discuss the matter with government officials this week. Speaking on broadcaster MagentaSport on the weekend, he conceded that surrendering Germany's hosting rights for the lucrative tournament was a possibility.

"I do not want to paint a black picture. I do not want to call the World Championship into question either. But of course, we at the DEB also have to consider the option of handing back this championship," he said.

Several other national ice hockey federations have expressed disappointment at the CAS decision, including those of Ukraine, Sweden, Finland, and Czechia.

The International Olympic Committee opened the door for Russian athletes to return to international competition when it lifted its ban of the Russian Olympic Committee in July. However, the IIHF had already decided to continue to exclude Russian teams for the 2026-27 season – over security concerns. The CAS decision – handed down after an appeal by Russia – found this reasoning was insufficiently proven.

The Kremlin's reaction to the ruling was, unsurprisingly, positive.

"Russia is returning to world hockey. This place rightfully belongs to us, and discrimination in hockey has been brought to an end," Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev told state television channel Vesti.

A boycott of the World Juniors, Men's World Championships or other tournaments by individual nations is now emerging as a real possibility.

"We are currently working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen said in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday evening.

"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.

By Tuesday afternoon, the Finland-led effort was gaining steam, with Sweden, Norway and Denmark making similar statements.

"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson said in a statement.

This came shortly after Norway said it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.

"Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors tournament.

There has been the suggestion, that having won this victory at the CAS, Russia's next focus could be on football, where its national and club teams remain excluded from international competitions.

Russian FA general secretary Maxim Mitrofanov told state news agency Tass that there "should be one rule for all."

World football's governing body FIFA allowed a Russia boys' team to play under its national flag in the inaugural Under-15 World Cup and Festival in Azerbaijan, which kicked off last week and ends on Saturday.

This article was originally published on November 2, 2026. It was updated on November 3 with the statement from the Finnish Ice Hockey Association. It was later updated with the statements from the Swedish, Norwegian and Danish federations.

But too many fart jokes hurt the experience.
