#300. Go foldable or go home: All the gadgets you can own that fold

Here’s an overview of some of the most notable folding gadget categories available today.

As someone who is a big believer in foldable phones, I've been eagerly tracking how gadget makers are exploring the use of flexible displays and novel designs across a wide range of categories. There's just something about a device that can transform into something else or shrink down to better fit into smaller spaces that's incredibly useful and satisfying. On top of that, I've also noticed that my travel tech kit has become increasingly populated with bendy gadgets, so I wanted to put together a short list of some of the most interesting foldable tech available today.

When it comes to laptops, depending on your definition, we've had foldable computers for more than 40 years. This dates all the way back to stuff like the Osborne 1 from 1981 and the Grid Compass from 1982, the latter of which is one of the earliest gadgets that still looks (vaguely) like the kind of clamshell PCs we use today. That said, when it comes to more contemporary foldables, I'm talking about things with more out-there designs — like laptops with dual displays, flexible screens or rollable/expandable panels.

Granted, while these types of laptops aren't super popular — often due to their price and unusual designs — there are more notebooks with dual or flexible displays on the market than you might realize. ASUS released the Zenbook 17 Fold back in 2022 before moving on to machines with two screens like the first- and second-gen Zenbook Duo. ASUS even made a gaming laptop with dual displays in the ROG Zephyrus Duo. HP created the Spectre Fold in 2023, but sadly hasn't revisited the category since. Then there's Lenovo, which might be the most prolific maker of laptops with rollable or flexible displays, including systems such as the ThinkPad X1 Fold, the ThinkBook Plus Gen 6 Rollable and more concept devices than you can shake a stick at.

While foldable smartphones are still relatively niche, you might be surprised to learn that they've been around for almost a decade, primarily dating back to the original Samsung Galaxy Fold. (You can make an argument that the Royale Flexpai came first, but seeing as how that line never really went anywhere, I'm giving credit to Samsung.) Since then, Samsung has continued iterating on the Z Fold family and the line is now in its eighth generation. Of course, new rivals have joined the fray from the likes of Google, Motorola and, most recently, Apple with the iPhone Duo. That's not even factoring a lot of the Chinese-made foldables that aren't officially available in the US or smaller flip-style devices.

However, now that pretty much every major smartphone manufacturer has its own take on a foldable handset, I hope momentum will pick up even more. For larger book-style devices, there's a lot to like about something that can serve as both a traditional smartphone and a small tablet that still fits in a purse or pocket. That said, even the least expensive large-format options still cost at least $1,800, so until OEMs can bring pricing down, cost will remain a prohibitive factor towards long-term adoption.

Computer mice might seem like a weird category when it comes to foldable gadgets, but there are examples that go back pretty far, like the original Microsoft Arc from 2008. Despite not having a ton of mainstream appeal, the company revised the Arc line several times over the past two decades with the most recent being the current Surface Arc Mouse. More recently, Logitech got in on the action with its first-ever foldable mouse: the Mobi Fold. And for people who want something with an even more engaging design, there are options like the myAir.0 OriMouse.

Here's another class of gadget where a foldable version might not have a major benefit. And in terms of pure audio quality, that's generally accurate. That said, there are countless headphones that feature headbands that can bend in half or collapse to make traveling just a bit easier. Some examples include Audio-Technica's M50x line, the Beats Solo 4 and more. Admittedly, if you are truly trying to travel light, earbuds may be a better option than full-sized cans.

While developing laptops with flexible displays, some companies like ASUS applied that tech to portable monitors as well, resulting in devices like the ZenScreen Fold. This model features very similar dimensions to the Zenbook 17 Fold, but without components like a CPU, GPU or RAM like you'd get on a notebook. It's an interesting gadget in theory, as it allows you to carry around a bigger screen than you'd normally be able to fit in a backpack or small suitcase. Unfortunately, with a starting price of $2,000, it was simply way too expensive for most people, and ASUS hasn't done much with the ZenScreen line since.

I also want to give honorable mentions to the Corsair Xeneon Flex and LG LX3. Even though they aren't portable, both of these are full desktop monitors that feature flexible displays that allow you to adjust their curvature to best suit your environment or other working conditions. While neither fold completely in half, the ability to transition from a flat display to something with up to an 800R or 900R curve still feels really futuristic, even though both of these displays were released in 2024.

Finally, there are other types of gadgets like dongles and wireless charging pads that fold up for improved portability. But at this point we're starting to get a bit in the weeds, especially when you consider that almost every type of cable is foldable in some manner. As for me, the foldable gadgets I'm currently using include the second-gen Zenbook Duo, a base Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the Logitech Mobi Fold. All together, I'd argue this represents one of the most adaptable tech loadouts on the market today. Between a smartphone that can turn into a small tablet, a laptop with two screens alongside a detachable keyboard and one of the most compact mice around, this kit can pretty much go anywhere and do anything that a regular person could ask of their devices.

#298. With World of Warcraft: Forever, Blizzard had to reconnect with what made WoW great in the first place

A lot of the team had to "unlearn" design habits they picked over the years.

After 13 years at Blizzard, Michael Nuthals faces what might just be the toughest challenge of his career yet: working on a familiar but different and highly anticipated version of World of Warcraft. As lead encounter designer, he's part of the team working on WoW: Forever. Announced at BlizzCon earlier this year, Forever is a sort of remaster of WoW designed to expand on the game's "Classic" era. It takes players back to Azeroth, the setting of the original 2004 game, before Blizzard over the course of 11 expansions took the game in the direction that it did. In the process, it imagines a "what if" scenario.

What if Blizzard had continued to expand Azeroth, instead of sending players to the Orc homeworld of Draenor and beyond with The Burning Crusade and later expansions? In Forever, there are more than 1,000 new quests for players to complete, many of them designed to continue story threads that were left unresolved in the original game. Additionally, there are new areas within Azeroth for players to explore — including Mount Hyjal, the site of one of Warcraft III's pivotal battles — in addition to fresh dungeons and raids. Blizzard has also rebalanced the game's classes and items, and built an entirely new global illumination lighting pipeline to make the game feel more atmospheric. Controversially, Forever will also feature a new race, the Skyborne Elves, who weren't in the original game.

The challenge Nuthals and his colleagues face is one of expectations. Nearly right from the moment Blizzard rereleased the original World of Warcraft in 2019, players have been asking the studio for a "Classic+" experience that expands the original game. The tricky thing is that, before Forever's announcement, every player had a different opinion on what an expanded rerelease should look like. Seemingly the only consensus was that the game shouldn't play anything like modern "retail" WoW. Realistically, there was never going to be a way Blizzard would find a way to please everyone with Forever, but it's still trying to create something fans both old and new can appreciate.

"I see it more as an opportunity — an opportunity to engage, to listen and show that we're listening," Nuthals says when asked about the weight of those expectations. With Forever, Blizzard recently concluded the largest beta in World of Warcraft's history. This is despite the fact players had to purchase one of Forever's premium bundles, which start at $60, to take part in the experience. Nuthals says Blizzard received "a lot of feedback" during the beta. He later admits one of the challenges of making Forever has been letting go of habits he learned working on the current version of WoW.

"Some of us had worked on the modern game for a long time, myself included. I come from modern, and it's almost like unlearning what you have learned," said Nuthals, who began working full-time on WoW ahead of 2014's Warlords of Draenor expansion. "We needed to understand what the DNA was [of WoW Classic], what the philosophies were, and to do that you just had to put it under your fingers and play." One way Nuthals and his colleagues did that was by revisiting the original game each week. Every Thursday morning, he and the rest of the encounter team would replay a classic dungeon like The Deadmines before jumping into one of the new dungeons they've created for Forever, such as Ruins of Lordaeron. Afterwards, they would ask themselves if those two dungeons felt like "they could live hand in glove?" and were connected.

"That was the development process," explains Nuthals. "We thought about what we want Forever to feel like, and we wanted it to feel like you wouldn't even know — like it was made in 2004. That was the vibe we were going for." Nuthals also credits the work Blizzard did with Season of Discovery, which was an offshoot of WoW Classic that saw the studio experiment with new class abilities, progression systems and dungeons within the confines of the original game.

"With Season of Discovery, we were pushing boundaries, exploring what Classic encounters could be. For Forever, we really looked back at the original Classic encounters and wanted to capture those, so we could provide a really authentic and nostalgic experience as players do these new raids," Nuthals said. As part of that process, the one thing he and the team kept coming back to is something Nuthals describes as the "strength, dexterity and intelligence" triangle of encounter design. Strength encounters reward the player for all the gear they've accumulated and their skill with their class, while dexterity ones test how well they can move and avoid hazards. Finally, intelligence-focused encounters test your understanding of a fight's mechanics and how much planning you've done.

"What we're trying to do with raids and dungeons is move toward gearing and planning, because Classic players really love that," said Nuthals. "'I overprepare, then I come in and crush the content.' That was the vibe we really wanted to hit." Part of how that philosophy will play out involves Forever's much advertised "horizontal" progression. With the new game, the studio has said it plans to keep the level cap at 60, meaning there won't be massive jumps in player power when the studio drops major new content. On paper at least, Blizzard appears committed to rewarding those who engage with and explore the game deeply.

"We're seeding the world with all these new items and things to chase, and in the future, having one of those items might pay off," said Nuthals. "We're thinking about those opportunities as we architect future raids and decide what bosses to introduce: making sure you feel smart for having pocketed something that comes in handy later. It feels good to use all that cool gear you went out and got."

Nuthals also said in the future Blizzard hopes to add new dungeons and zones, and that "not all of them will be max level." He added "there are areas players know about and want to explore, and there are opportunities for us to tell new stories in this space — taking what might have been a one-off quest name or something you found on a piece of paper and developing that story."

One question I didn't get a chance to ask Nuthals is what Blizzard will do if players, upon reaching 60, drop Forever and move onto other games. It's one thing for a studio to say it's committed to doing things differently with an MMO that doesn't take prey on player FOMO, and an entirely different thing to actually stick to that philosophy. We'll see how the future of Forever starts to unfold when the game arrives on November 4.

LSU star Angel Reese defended the gesture she aimed at Iowa Hawkeyes’ Caitlin Clark near the end of the Tigers’ first NCAA women’s basketball national championship victory on Sunday, saying “I don’t take disrespect lightly.”

Reese could be seen approaching Clark before moving her open hand in front of her face – popularized by WWE star John Cena to mean “you can’t see me” – before pointing to her ring finger in a gesture some interpreted as a reference to the place her newly-acquired championship ring might sit.

Caitlin Clark breaks records galore during historic March Madness run

Clark made a similar gesture to another player earlier in the tournament.

The gesture has sparked much debate, especially on social media. Some have criticized Reese, while others have defended her actions, highlighting how there was no public outrage in response to Clark’s gesture earlier in the tournament.

Sports journalist Jose de Jesus Ortiz called Reese’s actions “classless,” while former ESPN host Keith Olbermann called Reese an “idiot” for the gesture.

In the press conference after the victory, Reese referenced the difference in reaction she received as a result of her gesture as compared to the one Clark received.

“All year, I was critiqued for who I was. I don’t fit the narrative,” Reese said. “I don’t fit the box that y’all want me to be in. I’m too hood. I’m too ghetto. Y’all told me that all year. But when other people do it, and y’all don’t say nothing.

“So this is for the girls that look like me. For those that want to speak up for what they believe in. It’s unapologetically you. And that’s what I did it for tonight. It was bigger than me tonight. And Twitter is going to go into a rage every time.

“And I’m happy. I feel like I’ve helped grow women’s basketball this year. (…) I’m looking forward to celebrating and then next season.”

LSU beats Iowa to win its first NCAA women's basketball championship

In the post-game broadcast, Reese referenced the similar gesture Clark made to a Louisville opponent in the Elite Eight.

“Caitlin Clark is a hell of a player but I don’t take disrespect lightly,” Reese said. “She disrespected [LSU’s] Alexis [Morris] (…) and I wanted to pick her pocket. But I had a moment at the end of her game. I was in my bag, I was in my moment.”

After the Championship game, Clark herself said she didn’t notice anything at the time.

“I was just trying to get to the handshake line and shake hands and be grateful that my team was in that position,” Clark said in the post-game press conference. “All the credit in the world to LSU. They were tremendous. They deserve it. They had a tremendous season.

“(LSU head coach) Kim Mulkey coached them so, so well. She’s one of the best basketball coaches of all time, and it shows. She only said really kind things to me in the handshake line, so I’m very grateful of that too.

“But honestly I have no idea. I was just trying to spend the last few moments on the court with especially the five people that I’ve started 93 games with and relishing every second of that.”

LSU head coach Mulkey said she had “no clue” about what transpired.

Among those defending Reese on social media were ESPN’s Holly Rowe and former NBA star Etan Thomas.

“People hating on Angel Reese or Caitlin Clark. Stop. Unapologetically confident young women should be celebrated NOT hated. Get used to it,” Rowe wrote on Twitter.

Former Washington Wizards, Oklahoma City Thunder and Atlanta Hawks player Thomas wrote: “Hold on now!!!! It was cute when Caitlin Clark did it. Y’all didn’t have any issues with it at all. So don’t be all outraged and talking about class and sportsmanship when Angel Reese does the same thing. We’re not doing double standards here.”

Reese said the negative reaction on social media throughout the season has helped fuel her excellent season, having finished averaging 23.0 points and 15.4 rebounds in her first season with LSU after transferring from Maryland.

“Twitter can say what they want to say,” she said. “I love reading those comments. I have all the screenshots of what everybody has said about me all season. What are you going to say now?”

#296. Microsoft has listed some concrete ways that Windows 11 is getting better with 8GB of RAM

You should start noticing improved performance in a wide range of apps.

Microsoft has been doing a whole lot of shouting recently about how its 8GB Windows 11 PCs are performing better than ever, and it's now shared some more specific information about where you might start to notice a difference.

As previously revealed, the company claims that 8GB PCs are now up to 20 percent more responsive and 40 percent faster at multitasking. Windows is now able to retain up to 2GB more of your active data, rather than moving it to slower storage, which helps your PC stay more responsive as more tabs appear in your browser.

Since January, Microsoft says that interactions like opening Start, File Explorer and Settings, as well as searching and right-clicking, are all up to 20 percent more responsive, which it has achieved by directing your computer to reserve tasks like search indexing while you're working. Apps like Edge can also open up to 33 percent faster, while Efficiency Mode in Teams is turned on by default on 8GB PCs. This can speed up launch by up to 20 percent by dynamically reducing the load on your system resources.

Microsoft also says it has improved multitasking workflow speeds by up to 40 percent, which it tested by opening 20 tabs in Edge, as well as a 4K video, the Outlook app, File Explorer, and large files in Word PowerPoint and Excel. These were all left running once opened, and while 16GB of memory or more is still recommended for processor-hungry creatives who can afford it, you should be able to get more done quickly on a humble 8GB PC.

Apps like Word, PowerPoint, Excel and Outlook now use up to 360MB less RAM, which Microsoft says is down to improved efficiency, and even third-party apps like WhatsApp are hogging less memory than before. Other RAM-saving methods include Widgets that only load when opened and inactive tabs going to sleep after 15 minutes by default on 8GB configurations.

Aside from Windows itself, Microsoft says that newer processors are already playing their part. For example, a 2026 8GB Dell XPS 13 delivers over 90 percent faster multi-core CPU performance than its 2021 predecessor. The same 8GB model was able to largely match a 2021 configuration with twice as much memory in general CPU performance, web browsing, 4K video export and some AI tasks.

These performance and memory efficiency improvements require your Windows 11 PC to be running version 26H2 on the build 26300.9818 or later. Microsoft also recommends keeping all your apps updated and sometimes these improvements roll out through them.

#294. Beyond screens: Mercedes-Benz's new holographic heads-up display

After pioneering the passenger screen, Mercedes has designs on the windshield.

Do screens in cars represent luxury? Judging by the latest car interiors, the answer would seem to be an emphatic “yes.” Screens aren’t just getting larger; they are multiplying across the dashboard and morphing into different forms and concepts. Indeed, an interior’s screens are a pretty good indicator of what brand made the car—or at least how much the owner paid for it.

But is this actually what customers want? Are more screens really better? And even if they are, luxury car features inevitably trickle down to cheaper, more mainstream offerings, and screens can only get so big. That leaves luxury automakers with another question to answer: “What’s next?”

Mercedes-Benz is working on a new display alternative that could provide an answer. For now, it’s known as the holographic display. Forget the images from Star Trek and Star Wars that just popped into your head, though. It’s effectively a more advanced form of heads-up display, or HUD.

Whereas a traditional HUD projects images onto the windshield glass, the holographic display has two main components. It still uses a projector, but its key element is a special transparent film laminated into the glass. The film uses holographic optical elements, or “super-small mirrors,” as Mercedes development engineer Lena Hees described them, that selectively reflect the light emitted by the projector, keeping the image visible even in direct sunlight while hiding it from the driver’s view.

Today, the passenger-side touchscreens in Mercedes and other luxury vehicles rely on driver-monitoring cameras or screen polarization to keep the driver from seeing what is playing on the passenger side.

Speaking of passenger screens, the holographic display is clearly being considered as a future alternative or replacement for this technology. Although screens in cars are increasingly ubiquitous, a recent JD Power study indicated that car owners classify passenger screens as “not necessary” and have generally negative opinions about them. Mercedes has clearly observed similar opinions but for slightly different reasons.

“We have customers who like the Hyperscreen,” said development engineer Maximilian Hilger of the pillar-to-pillar screen found in an increasing number of Mercedes models. “But there are others who want to maintain luxury materials.”

In other words, the massive screen design doesn’t seem as luxurious as the pillar-to-pillar bands of wood or other materials found in previous-generation models. And that’s not an opinion isolated to Mercedes’ customers.

New Mercedes chief design officer Bastian Baudy recently told German magazine Auto Motor Sport that “Materiality and haptics must remain tangible—with switches, buttons, and intuitive controls. Real materials are at the heart of Mercedes: metal, wood.”

Mercedes CEO Ola Källenius went further, grouping interior quality and materials among the brand’s “forever values,” along with safety and maintaining what a Mercedes is like to drive.

That presents conflicting priorities, however.

“Yes, you need to have all the [technology] that a customer could ever dream of and wants,” Källenius told Ars. “But you need to package it in an aesthetically pleasing way. That’s also part of it.”

That brings us back to the holographic display. Keep in mind that the photos in this article show early prototypes I saw at Mercedes’ research facilities in Sindelfingen, Germany. The prototype projector sits inside a rather crude, trapezoidal hole dug into the dash of a right-hand-drive, pre-2027 S-Class. It’s also loud, with a cooling fan whirring like a laptop visiting too many junk-filled websites.

The production version would have a much smaller projector opening than those of the prototype and existing heads-up displays. Manual Holstein, a manager working in Mercedes research for future displays, indicated that the projector could be small enough to be hidden behind wood or metal trim pieces. Holstein also said you won’t hear a fan in the production model and that the resolution would improve.

The resolution is certainly considerably better than any current head-up display, including Mercedes’ own, which features augmented reality elements. Full-color, commercial-like videos of the C-Class Electric played during the demonstration, and the display was sufficiently bright, even though Holstein said the prototype was operating at just 20 percent of its maximum brightness.

Issues remain, however. The resolution may be good compared to the arrows, script, and graphics of a current HUD, but it’s poor when compared to a passenger touchscreen. The video’s contrast was also too high, and as you can see in the photos, the picture was distorted into a narrow height due to the angle of the windshield. Frankly, no one would choose to watch anything on it over a phone, tablet, or conventional passenger screen. It needs to improve by orders of magnitude before becoming a viable alternative.

Again, though, this is just a prototype. Holstein said the holographic film size, or “eyebox,” can be made much bigger and be raised higher than the HUD-like height of the prototype. He also dismissed the distortion as a problem unique to the prototype.

Imagine nearly half the windshield transformed into a virtual screen that’s visible only to the passenger. Beyond videos or other entertainment, Mercedes envisions the holographic display highlighting points of interest in the view through the windshield. A similar display could be placed on the driver side, showing situational information, enabling video calls, or providing entertainment when parked. In the future, it could even let drivers watch things other than the road when Mercedes’ Level 3 autonomous driving system allows them to take their eyes off it. At the very least, the technology could replace today’s HUDs and their larger projector boxes.

Having experienced the prototype while the car was moving, I also think the holographic display could help prevent the motion sickness that can come from staring at a passenger screen while the car is moving. The higher screen angle and ability to see more of the outside world beyond created a notably different visual experience.

Of course, the question remains: “Is this what customers want?”

If the JD Power survey found that customers don’t care about passenger touchscreens, will they be any more enthusiastic about holographic video displays? That seems doubtful. But that’s just as much of an open question as whether the production version will actually live up to its promises.

There’s also another matter: What, exactly, defines luxury? Before Bastian Baudy took over as Mercedes’ chief design officer this year, his predecessor and former boss Gordon Wagener echoed Källenius’ thoughts about the direction of the brand’s interiors. He was considerably blunter, though.

“Screens are not luxury,” Wagener told ABC News. “You have a better—and bigger—TV at home, right? And every car has a big screen. So we have to create luxury beyond the screen. That’s why I talk about craftsmanship and sophistication.”

If the holographic display lets automakers emphasize traditional design and materials while still offering unique technology, it could be a promising way forward.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#290. Google says students in schools that ban AI won't have access to Search

Gotta get those AI user numbers up somehow.

Google seems to have shoved as many AI features into as many of its products as it can over the last few years in an attempt to justify the tens of billions of dollars it has plowed into the technology. It appears to be making another attempt to bump up its AI user numbers by issuing an ultimatum to schools: enable AI features or students won't be able to use Search.

In one of several blog posts Google published Tuesday about its education efforts, it said it believes educators should have control over the use of AI in schools. "After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search," Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager for education, wrote. "Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on." Google clarified to Engadget that  administrators will be able to enable these products individually, and that it's not an all-or-nothing deal.

The company plans to roll out these updated controls in the coming months as it walks back a change it made this summer. In August, Google enabled certain AI features by default in the Classroom learning platform. That shift prompted a backlash from educators, as The New York Times reported, leading Google to reverse course.

However, Phillips told the publication that "Search and AI are deeply integrated." If a school bans AI tools, students "will not have access to Search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available."

Chromebooks and Google's education apps are widely used in schools, particularly in the US. If school districts don't play by Google's new rules, they may have to consider alternative search engines (and perhaps other devices and digital learning platforms) going forward.

Several jurisdictions have limited access to generative AI in schools. In September, New York City placed a one-year moratorium on the use of such tools in public schools for students through eighth grade. The Los Angeles public school system enacted a similar ban that same month. Last week, New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a law that bans AI companies from offering certain chatbot features to minors.

In school districts and jurisdictions that do allow the use of AI, Google offers a tool called Guided Learning, which is available globally in Classroom starting today. Rather than giving students the answer to a question or activity assigned by their teacher, Guided Learning (which was already available in the Gemini app) breaks problems down into step-by-step explanations and offers interactive features like quizzes. Google suggested it's akin to one-on-one tutoring.

The company said it's adding Guided Learning tools to Search in student accounts as well, ostensibly as a measure to limit cheating. "When our systems understand a student is looking for certain types of homework help, Search will walk them through the topic or problem step by step," Phillips wrote. "For example, if a student pastes a complex physics problem or asks for help writing a book report in Search, they'll see prompts to help them think critically and work through the concepts, without going directly to the answer."

The company will test this approach in select schools in the US starting this month before a broader expansion. In the school version of Guided Learning, teachers will be able to access transcripts of chatbot interactions on student accounts.

#288. How to choose the right gaming monitor for you

Refresh rates, size and screen technology all play a part.

Choosing the right gaming monitor is a lot like choosing the right outfit. You wouldn't wear the same thing to the gym as you would to the opera, while lifting weights in a tuxedo would inconvenience you and damage the tux. Similarly, a monitor that works great for one PC or console isn't necessarily the best fit for another and gamers who enjoy competitive shooters should look for different options than those who enjoy visually rich single-person narratives.

Only you can figure out exactly which monitor you should buy. To do that, you'll first need to understand which specs best suit your needs. Modern monitors have a lot more to them than resolution and frame rate. Different display panel types suit different uses and picture quality can vary between models. A quick crash course on the basics will get you ready to shop for the monitor you'll be happiest with in the long run.

Before we dive into specs, the first thing to consider when picking a gaming monitor is the existing hardware you'll pair it with. If your PC is decked out with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 or 5080, you can run games on the bleeding edge of performance and have real reasons to consider a top-shelf monitor with a 4K panel and an ultra-high refresh rate. On the other hand, if you're plugging the monitor into an older or lower-powered GPU, consider the performance you'll actually get in the games you play. If you aren't routinely seeing frame rates above, say, 90 fps, there's no reason to invest in a 240Hz monitor. Resolution and refresh rate move in opposite directions, so if you play competitive shooters and esports titles like Valorant, it's best to sacrifice pixels for higher frames, whereas players of visually rich first-person titles like Control: Resonant can make the opposite trade-off or find a balance in the middle.

Once you know the spec range you're looking for, you can move on to other concerns such as panel type, HDR and brightness support, port selection and VRR technologies like G-Sync. Size and resolution are personal preferences. Resolution is tied to graphical performance, but there are reasons other than gaming to consider a 1440p or 4K display. If you do a lot of photo or video editing, or if you watch a lot of video, a higher resolution can be worthwhile. Size is related to resolution, in the sense that the smaller of two monitors with the same resolution will have a higher pixel density  — a finer level of image detail, which can be measured in pixels per inch (PPI).

Esports players often prefer smaller monitors around 24 inches in order to see everything at once, while single-player gamers who value immersion may gravitate toward 27 inches or higher. Larger displays also support multitasking better, but work best when you sit farther back. You'll also need to consider your ideal aspect ratio. A squatter shape is better for productivity tasks, but 16:9 widescreen is the de facto aspect ratio for gaming. Some gamers enjoy ultra-widescreen monitors to fill their peripheral vision, but in games where HUD information is crucial, ultrawide displays can force you to look away from the action.

Refresh rate is often considered the most essential specification when choosing a monitor, and should be the first thing you settle on. As noted above, your GPU should dictate this. Monitors are now shipping with up to 1,000 Hz in lower-resolution modes, at which point you'd question whether you can see the difference even if you could push your hardware that far.

The average PC gamer in September 2026 was running an RTX 5070, 5060, 4060 or even a 3060, according to the Steam Hardware Survey. Accordingly, the sweet spot for the average gamer is likely to land somewhere from 144Hz to 240Hz on a 1440p or 1080p panel. If you have a similar configuration but want to play competitive, lightweight games, you may want to look for a 1080p panel with a significantly higher frame rate. Players of these titles with top-end hardware (such as an RTX 5080 or 5090) can look for 1440p or 4K panels at any refresh rate.

That said, only you can determine the real-world frame rates you're getting on your hardware. One way to do that is to turn on the Steam, NVIDIA, or Xbox in-game overlays while playing and enable the small heads-up frame rate counter they offer. You can also use a benchmarking tool like 3DMark and some games, including Cyberpunk 2077, have built-in benchmark tests. Even if your current monitor can't reach high frame rates, you'll still see a readout showing how many frames per second your graphics card is producing.

After playing multiple games that are representative of your general interests, note where you saw the highest frame rates. Unless you plan to upgrade your GPU in the next several years, there's no need to overspend on a monitor with an unachievably high refresh rate for your system.

If you're looking for a monitor to use with a console, it's worth noting that even the best current-generation consoles like the PlayStation 5 Pro or Xbox Series X don't exceed refresh rates of 120 Hz. That means you're better off putting your money toward a larger or higher-resolution monitor instead of buying a panel with blistering speeds you'll never utilize.

After determining the refresh rate, resolution and aspect ratio ideal to your setup, the biggest choice you'll make is the type of panel your monitor is fitted with. For most gamers, the two best choices are OLED and Fast IPS, in that order.

OLED is well known for its technically infinite contrast ratios, accurate colors and near-instant response times. Because each pixel is self-emissive, it produces its own light rather than relying on a backlight; OLED pixels simply do not illuminate where an image is truly black, meaning they stay black rather than turning dark grey in the way LCD panels do. That makes them ideal for gaming, especially if you value HDR performance.

However, OLED displays have their drawbacks. They require more care to prevent OLED burn-in, a condition in which leaving a static image on screen for too long leaves a permanent ghost of that image on the screen. Newer OLEDs address this with pixel-shifting that slightly moves the picture around and pixel-cleaning cycles that help keep wear and tear even across the display. If you're the sort of person who leaves your monitor on for hours when you're not using it, an OLED will force you to change that behavior.

OLEDs are also dimmer than LCDs and are consequently worse in well-lit environments. Some manufacturers offer matte coatings on their OLED models, which can help, but these displays look best in a dim or dark room. Text fringing is another issue, as is motion flicker and while the latest generation of OLED has come a long way in minimizing them, gamers who also work with documents and spreadsheets should take those issues into consideration before paying the higher cost for an OLED. Thatcost is perhaps the biggest downside, as even entry-level OLEDs start around $400 in late 2026. If you do choose to go OLED, scout for sales.

LCD panels lack the sheer wow factor of OLED, but they are more versatile. There are a range of LCD types, but Fast IPS is generally the best for gaming. IPS panels deliver excellent colors, great viewing angles and they have very consistent performance. However, regular IPS can introduce significant motion blur, which is reduced in a Fast IPS panel. For users who game in bright environments, plan to do productivity work on their gaming PC, or are on a budget, Fast IPS is an easy recommendation.

Gaming on a PC can be uneven, and one of the most frustrating issues you'll commonly encounter is screen tearing. This occurs when the GPU cranks out frames at a different rate than the monitor shows them, so the display shows parts of two frames at the same time. Substantial tearing can completely ruin a gaming session, but there's a surefire fix for screen tearing: variable refresh rate (VRR) technology. NVIDIA G-Sync, AMD FreeSync and the generic Adaptive Sync are all examples of VRR.

For a deeper dive, check out our article on screen tearing and how to fix it, but the bottom line is that you'll want G-Sync or FreeSync on your monitor. By now, it's an industry standard and you won't need to spend much extra money, if any, to get a monitor that has one of those two certifications.

G-Sync can cost extra because it uses a hardware module inside the monitor. However, NVIDIA has certified plenty of monitors as G-Sync Compatible. This means that a monitor doesn't need that module to work with G-Sync. Many FreeSync monitors are G-Sync Compatible.

Console gamers can completely ignore G-Sync, as no console uses an NVIDIA GPU. The Xbox Series X and Series S support FreeSync because of their AMD hardware, while the PlayStation 5 and PS5 Pro support only HDMI 2.1 VRR.

Regardless of your hardware, VRR only works with the right cable. Make sure you're using a cable with at least DisplayPort 1.2a. If you're using HDMI, some HDMI 1.4 and 2.0 connections will support VRR, but the most robust support comes with HDMI 2.1 onward.

#286. AO3s outage has exposed a growing divide between fanfiction authors and readers

The fanfiction is gone, but the fandom discourse is thriving.

It's been six days since Archive of Our Own (AO3), the internet's beloved fanfiction repository, went offline following a reported security incident. What was initially supposed to be routine maintenance has turned into a potentially weeks-long disruption, leaving millions of readers without their favorite stories and writers without a place to publish them. Naturally, the internet has responded with the kind of collective meltdown you'd expect from people suddenly deprived of their favorite fictional relationships.

There have been memes, dramatic declarations of withdrawal, and even makeshift survival guides filled with downloaded fanfiction. Fans of Heated Rivalry, in particular, have been sharing Google Drive archives to ensure that the adventures of Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov remain accessible during these trying times.

Not all of these efforts have been welcomed, however. One since-deleted Google Drive containing more than 200 fanfics spanning multiple fandoms began circulating online, prompting some authors to question why their work was being redistributed without their knowledge or consent. While readers saw these collections as a way to keep fanfiction accessible during the outage, some writers saw their stories being shared without anyone bothering to ask permission.

Then there are the more blatant attempts to capitalize on AO3's absence, including vibe-coded clone sites attempting to profit from fanfiction originally published for free. One such site was reportedly hit with more than 2,000 takedown notices from authors in a single day.

And just like that, what began as a collective fandom crisis turned into a familiar argument about ownership, consent, and what readers owe the people who write the stories they love.

It's a debate that has been simmering within fandom communities for years, fueled by disagreements over reader expectations, unsolicited criticism, and the harassment of fan creators. But the AO3 outage has brought a new urgency to these conversations, exposing a fundamental tension within fanfiction culture: What happens when stories created and shared freely, out of love for a fandom, begin to be treated as content to which readers are entitled?

To understand why this conversation matters, it's important to understand what makes AO3 different from most of the internet.

Founded by fans and operated by the nonprofit Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), AO3 was created to give fanworks a permanent home, free from commercial pressures and the threat of censorship. Today, it houses more than 18.8 million fanworks, according to the New York Times. There's no algorithm deciding which stories deserve attention, no advertising generating revenue from readers, and no financial compensation for the writers who collectively contribute millions of words to the archive.

Fanfiction has historically operated within what's often described as a gift economy. Writers create stories because they love the source material, the characters, and the communities that form around them. Readers reciprocate through comments, recommendations, fan art, and other forms of engagement. The exchange isn't financial, but that doesn't mean it lacks value.

In many ways, that relationship is what makes fanfiction special. A writer can spend months crafting a 200,000-word slow-burn romance about two characters who barely interact in canon, publish it for free, and find an audience of people who are just as emotionally invested in those characters as they are.

There are no publishing contracts or sales targets. There is simply the pleasure of creating something and sharing it with people who understand why it matters.

But that relationship can become complicated when readers begin to treat freely shared creative work as a product they're entitled to receive.

The frustration some fanfiction writers express isn't necessarily about readers wanting more stories. Most writers want their work to be read, appreciated, and discussed. The debate emerges when enthusiasm turns into expectation.

I saw this firsthand recently when I posted a TikTok responding to a claim that the quality of fanfiction has declined. The comments quickly filled with writers expressing frustration over what they perceived as a growing sense of entitlement among readers. "The entitlement in complaining about the 'decline in quality' when reading free fiction is unreal omg," one commenter wrote.

The sentiment extends well beyond debates over writing quality. Anyone who has spent enough time in fandom has probably encountered some version of this dynamic — readers demanding updates on unfinished works, criticizing authors for abandoning stories, or leaving comments that read more like customer complaints than responses to something another person created for free.

Of course, readers are allowed to have opinions. Not every fanfiction is going to be well-written, and not every creative decision deserves universal praise. Criticism has always been part of fandom, too. But there's a difference between discussing a story and treating its author like a content provider who has failed to deliver.

And that relationship can feel particularly one-sided when readers consume stories without engaging with the people who create them. On AO3, leaving kudos or a comment is one of the simplest ways to show appreciation for a writer's work. Neither is required, of course, but those small interactions are part of what makes fanfiction feel like a community rather than just another endless library of content. Downloading a story to read offline isn't inherently a problem. But when the act of reading becomes entirely passive, something gets lost in the exchange.

It raises a broader question about whether the habits we've developed as consumers of digital content are changing how we participate in fandom. We're accustomed to creators posting on schedules, streaming platforms offering endless entertainment, and algorithmic feeds serving up a constant stream of things to watch, read, and react to. There's always something new to consume, and notably, an expectation that there always will be.

But fanfiction doesn't operate on those same terms. At least, it was never intended to. A reader might spend hours immersed in a story without ever considering the person who spent weeks, months, or even years writing it. And when that story ends on a cliffhanger, it's easy to forget that the person responsible for the next chapter has a life outside the fictional universe they've created.

That doesn't make readers inherently entitled, nor does it mean writers are above criticism. But when we begin to approach fanfiction with the same expectations we bring to streaming services and social media, we risk losing sight of what makes it different in the first place. These stories aren't products commissioned by a platform or created to meet an audience's demand. They're personal expressions of creativity, shared freely by people who love something enough to imagine what else it could become.

And the relationship between writers and readers can be deeply rewarding. Most fanfiction writers are readers themselves, participating in the same fandoms and eagerly awaiting updates from their favorite authors. Writing and reading aren't opposing sides of fandom. They're interconnected parts of the same creative ecosystem.

In interviews with 404 Media following the outage, writers described how much AO3's comment sections mean to them. For some, comments provide encouragement during creative slumps. For others, they're a reminder that someone on the other side of the screen is connecting with a story they've poured so much of themselves into.

One writer even expressed hope that the outage would encourage readers to tell their favorite authors how much they'd missed their work once AO3 returned, saying, "I do kind of hope that the extended outage serves as a sort of wake-up call to anyone who's been taking AO3 for granted lately."

For now, AO3 remains offline while OTW investigates the security incident. In its Oct. 30 update, the organization said that no works, bookmarks, or kudos had been deleted. However, it couldn't yet rule out the possibility that user account information had been compromised. The nonprofit expects restoration to take at least two weeks, possibly as long as four, with limited functionality possibly returning sooner.

In the meantime, fans are still finding ways to keep reading, writing, and connecting outside the archive.

AO3's absence has made its importance impossible to ignore. It's more than a place to find a 300,000-word enemies-to-lovers AU at two in the morning. It's an archive of fandom history and a community sustained by people who love these fictional worlds enough to keep expanding them.

And when AO3 eventually returns, perhaps readers will have a little more appreciation for the people who make those stories possible.

#285. Don't throw away your old AirPods — do this instead

Instead of getting rid of your old AirPods, replace the battery and give them a new purpose.

AirPods are built to last, and they usually work for years before they stop functioning completely. You'll likely buy new AirPods before your old ones stop working, though they may no longer sound brand-new.

So what should you do with your old AirPods? Throwing them in the trash is something you certainly shouldn't do; Apple discourages this because of the lithium-ion batteries inside them. The good news is that, depending on the problem, Apple can fix your buds for a reasonable fee. Your old AirPods can become good backup earbuds, or even a gift for a friend or family member.

If battery performance is the only real problem, it's likely worth getting a replacement before buying new AirPods. Even if you've already bought a new pair, replacing the batteries in your old earbuds will make them better for someone else.

But unlike an iPhone or iPad, Apple won't open AirPods to replace their batteries. Instead, the company recycles your old AirPods and gives you new ones, charging you a lower price per earbud. For most AirPods, a battery replacement costs $49 per earbud, so $98 if you need to replace the battery in both. That's much cheaper than buying new AirPods Pro, for example, which cost $249. For the higher-end AirPods Max, a battery replacement costs $79, which is also much cheaper than paying $549 for new headphones.

If you have AppleCare, you may be eligible for a free battery replacement if any battery falls below 80 percent of its original capacity. And if any battery in your AirPods fails while they're still under warranty, Apple will replace them for free. Some independent repair shops can replace the battery inside AirPods, but this requires cutting them open and gluing them back together. You might end up saving some money, but they won't look as good as new — not to mention that they'll also lose their water and sweat resistance.

If you've lost one of your earbuds or the charging case, Apple offers replacements for them. Prices vary depending on the model; for the Pro line, a new earbud costs $89 and a new case costs $99. For standard AirPods, it's $69 to replace one bud and between $59 and $79 to replace the case.

It's thus usually worth it for the more expensive AirPods Pro, but not so much for the base AirPods. The latest AirPods 5 cost $129 from Apple, and it's not hard to find them for a little less at other stores.

Instead of tossing your old AirPods into a drawer, there are plenty of other ways to put them to good use. Earbuds that still hold a decent charge could be worth something. Apple doesn't offer trade-in credit for AirPods, but buyback services like Back Market will give you some money for them. Selling them directly on places like eBay or Facebook Marketplace usually pays more.

Or you can simply give them to a friend or family member, so they'll only have to pay for a battery replacement if needed. If you pass them on, be sure to clean the AirPods and remove them from your Apple account — new ear tips will be much appreciated.

Keeping them around is also suitable if they still work fine. Have your old AirPods ready as backup earbuds in case you lose your new ones, leave them somewhere or simply need another set when your usual pair runs out of battery. Some people prefer to use old AirPods as gym earbuds so their new ones don't get covered in sweat. If you like to sleep with your AirPods in, using your old ones can avoid draining the battery on the new ones. Or you might devote them for listening to your Roku at night via Bluetooth.

In case your old AirPods are truly dead and you don't want to spend money on them, Apple will recycle them for free. You don't even need to take them to an Apple Store, since Apple provides a prepaid shipping label in certain regions. You won't get paid for them, but at least your earbuds will be disposed of properly.

#284. Chelsea searches for new manager as Premier League breaks record for most sackings in a single season

It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.

The club’s new ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.

More than $600 million was spent on bringing big-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.

Chelsea has spent over $600 million on new signings. Here's why that's significant

But, on Sunday, the club announced that it had sacked its manager after an underwhelming spell in charge.

Potter managed to win just 10 of the 28 league matches this season and leaves the team 11th in the Premier League table.

In recent weeks, players had looked a shadow of their former selves and many fans had lost confidence that Potter’s plan for the club could ever work.

Eventually, after previously sticking by its manager, Blues ownership agreed.

“On behalf of everyone at the club, we want to thank Graham sincerely for his contribution to Chelsea,” the club’s co-owners Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali said in a statement.

“We have the highest degree of respect for Graham as a coach and as a person. He has always conducted himself with professionalism and integrity and we are all disappointed in this outcome.”

In his previous role as Brighton manager, Potter was given time to stamp his identity on the squad.

The club was punching above its weight financially and, as a result, carefully selected new signings which would compliment Potter’s style of play.

The approach paid off as the team became an established Premier League outfit which has gone on to greater things this season – the Seagulls currently sit sixth in the league and in the UEFA Conference League qualification spot.

At Chelsea, it seemed the complete opposite.

As was the case under previous owner Roman Abramovich, the club expected instant results and used its financial weight to sign a number of high-profile names, including the likes of Enzo Fernández and Mykhailo Mudryk.

Despite his impressive CV, Potter had never managed superstars and suddenly found himself in a changing room with multiple.

The scatter gun approach to recruitment also left the team lacking balance and organization with Potter failing to get a tune out of a team busting with talent.

In truth, many had raised an eyebrow when Potter, inexperienced at the very top level, was chosen to replace Thomas Tuchel as manager.

Despite falling out of favor with fans by the end of his tenure, Tuchel had guided Chelsea to the Champions League title in 2021 and is still considered by many as one of the best coaches in the world.

The German has gone on to sign with Bavarian giant Bayern Munich through the 2024/25 season and recently told reporters he needed “quite a bit of time to distance himself from Chelsea” because leaving the club had hurt him.

Bayern Munich sacks manager Julian Nagelsmann, appoints Thomas Tuchel

“Todd [Boehly] said he would be different to Roman [Abramovich],” former Liverpool player and current pundit Jamie Carragher wrote on Twitter.

“I feel for Graham Potter, but it was inevitable. You don’t change Tuchel for Potter. Ridiculous decision to start with.”

With 10 games left in the league and a Champions League quarterfinal against Real Madrid on the horizon, Chelsea still has plenty to play for.

Assistant coach Bruno Saltor will take over on an interim basis, but Boehly and his team must now look for a long-term replacement capable – and willing – to bring order to Chelsea’s chaos.

Potter’s sacking is yet another sign of just how transient managers can be in the top-flight of English football, especially when results aren’t instantaneous.

There has now been a record 12 sackings in the Premier League so far this season, with Potter leaving his position the same day Leicester boss Brendan Rodgers was sacked from his.

The previous record was 10 manager changes in a single season, set in four other campaigns, most recently in 2017/18.

#283. EPA throws in the towel on policing air pollution from factory farms

Critics say EPA is effectively abandoning Clean Air Act enforcement at factory farms.

The Environmental Protection Agency late last week announced it would end a 20-plus-year effort to develop methods to monitor air pollution from factory farms, effectively shuttering the agency’s stop-and-start attempts to regulate the potentially pollutant-spewing facilities under the Clean Air Act.

The announcement came just days before the midterm elections and was characterized by the agency as a long-awaited reprieve for farmers, a historically important constituency for Trump and the Republican Party.

When tens of thousands of animals are packed into one place, pollution from their waste is blown from ventilation fans or emanates from giant lagoons of liquid effluent. Livestock facilities emit fine particulate matter, ammonia, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, and volatile organic compounds, all contributing to a toxic mix. Research has shown that emissions from these operations are a major cause of air pollution, causing nearly 12,700 deaths in the United States a year.

Strictly speaking, concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs, are required to get permits under the Clean Air Act and report emissions of these pollutants under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability and Act and the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act. But through a deal crafted in tandem with the EPA and the livestock industry, they’ve been given amnesty from doing so for more than 20 years.

The arrangement goes back to the early 2000s when the agency attempted to prosecute CAFOs for exceeding limits on some of these pollutants. The industry pushed back, arguing there was no adequate way of measuring them. So the agency worked with industry groups to develop what was dubbed the Air Consent Agreement, through which the EPA granted thousands of CAFOs safe harbor from legal action in exchange for their participation in a study that was funded by the industry.

The goal of the study, the agency said, was to develop tools and models that CAFOs could use to “determine whether they emit pollutants at levels that require them to apply for permits under the CAA or submit notifications under CERCLA or EPCRA” and “produce a scientifically sound basis for measuring and estimating air emissions” from these facilities.

But since the adoption of the agreement in 2005, the agency has failed to produce any air “emissions estimating methodologies,” even prompting a 2017 report from the agency’s Office of Inspector General that faulted it for slow-walking the process.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration and Congress have also gutted reporting requirements for factory farms to report air pollutants under CERCLA, also known as the Superfund Act, and EPCRA.

“As EPA has been saying it’s proceeding with this plan, it’s been dismantling all of its own tools to regulate emissions,” said Tarah Heinzen, the legal director for the advocacy group Food & Water Watch, which has tracked the proceedings from the beginning and filed dozens of lawsuits attempting to push regulators to control pollution from CAFOs. “Now it has announced it has no intention, basically, of ever holding factory farms accountable under the Clean Air Act, either.”

In its October 30 announcement, the agency noted that in the two decades since the study, known as the National Air Emissions Monitoring Study, was conducted, many farms have modernized their barns and manure systems.

“Good science requires good data, and these data are too old and too limited to support methods that farms could rely on,” said Abigale Tardif, the acting assistant administrator for the agency’s Office of Air and Radiation, in a statement. “We would rather tell farmers that plainly than issue numbers we cannot stand behind.”

Rob Brenneman, president of the National Pork Producers Council, which has long pushed for the decision, said in a statement: “This move confirms what farmers have long known: Every farm is different, and there is no one-size-fits-all model to apply to them.”

Heinzen noted that the agency’s decision simply means that this administration has no intention of regulating air emissions from CAFOs, but for now, the Clean Air Act still requires permits for facilities that exceed emissions thresholds. The amnesty granted to these facilities will no longer be in effect now that the agreement has concluded.

“There’s no EPA-issued methodology to estimate emissions,” she said. “That doesn’t mean that there aren’t good studies out there of emissions from different types of animal feeding operations that can be used.”

Heinzen pointed to California, which has models for livestock emissions that it uses to enforce its own air regulations. “We just don’t have one set of national emissions factors from EPA,” Heinzen said. “That does not absolve these factory farms from their obligation to comply with federal law.”

Still, under this administration, it’s clear air emissions from factory farms won’t be measured and monitored any time soon. “No one’s going to estimate anything,” Heinzen noted. “As EPA said in its press release, we’re certainly not about to try to enforce the law.”

The Air Compliance Agreement did not extend to methane. The US livestock industry is the single-biggest source of methane in the country, but Congress effectively blocks livestock facilities from reporting methane emissions in annual spending bills.

Georgina Gustin covers agriculture for Inside Climate News, and has reported on the intersections of farming, food systems and the environment for much of her journalism career. Her work has won numerous awards, including the John B. Oakes Award for Distinguished Environmental Journalism, and she was twice named the Glenn Cunningham Agricultural Journalist of the Year, once with ICN colleagues. She has worked as a reporter for The Day in New London, Conn., the St. Louis Post-Dispatch and CQ Roll Call, and her stories have appeared in The New York Times, Washington Post and National Geographic’s The Plate, among others. She is a graduate of the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism and the University of Colorado at Boulder.

This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News.

#282. How to make your older Android phones last longer

There's no getting around it: New phones are expensive. Regardless of brand or platform, a brand-new phone is going to cost a pretty penny thanks to the global memory shortage and its subsequent price increases that have pushed the forecasted average smartphone price up to more than $580 in 2026, nearly 28 percent higher than last year, according to IDC data.

Sure, you can look into the latest mobile carrier promotions, like X dollars off or a free new phone when you switch to Y carrier. But if you think a mobile carrier is giving you a brand-new phone for free, you might want to read the contract's fine print more closely. You're probably paying for it through financing or expensive data plans.

If you're thinking about replacing your old Android phone, you might want to reconsider shelling out hundreds of (or even over a thousand) dollars for a new one. Just a few inexpensive and free solutions can prolong the life of your Android smartphone so you can get even more out of it.

If your Android phone doesn't charge as quickly or is gobbling up battery power at a faster rate than when you first bought the phone, a degraded battery is likely the cause. A degrading battery also impacts the phone's performance, because it can't provide the quick bursts of power the phone's processor needs to run certain tasks or apps. This results in slow loading, annoying lag and even total freezing.

Unfortunately, many phone users attribute the lackluster performance to the phone itself and wind up paying hundreds for a new model. But a new battery may do the trick, at a fraction of the price — especially if your older Android phone has a back that snaps or slides off for easy battery replacement. A quick Amazon search for Samsung Galaxy replacement lithium-ion batteries delivers hundreds of options in the $10 to $20 range. If the back of your Android smartphone is sealed, you may need to buy a DIY repair kit (typically $60 or less) or have it replaced professionally (usually no more than $80 at a local repair shop). But even the high end of those costs pales in comparison to the price of a new phone.

Making sure your battery is optimized can also help. Your Android phone should be equipped with a battery-saving mode, which disables or adapts some of the phone's features — such as screen brightness — to cut back on battery usage. Some Google Pixel phones offer battery optimization as well as Adaptive Battery, which limits the amount of time your less-used apps run and then learns your app usage patterns to optimize battery life. And many Samsung phones have similar features that put your less frequently used apps into sleep mode to save juice.

Another tip is to keep your phone charged to between 20 and 80 percent throughout the day. And, yes, that includes overnight. Doing so, according to LiTime, drastically reduces the battery's exposure to chemical stress, which can help your phone's battery last between two and three times longer than a battery that is consistently charged to 100 percent.

Sometimes the most effective solutions are the simplest ones. Protecting your older Android phone with a sturdy case and a screen protector can help prolong its life. No, the phone may not look as sleek and cool inside a rubber or silicone case. But if your aim is to squeeze as much life out of your old Android phone as possible, aesthetics understandably aren't your top priority. A case will improve your grip on the phone while providing shock absorption should it fall to the ground.

Besides, there are some nice-looking phone cases out there. And for an older Android phone model, a solid case isn't going to cost you much. You know what will, though? Buying a new phone to replace the one that now has a useless shattered screen because it dropped to the ground and wasn't protected by a case.

It's always a good idea to keep your phone updated with the latest operating system, especially when it comes to security. Most updates offer security patches to close up any potential vulnerabilities to hackers. Also, many of the apps on your phone will need the newest Android OS version to remain compatible and fully functional.

Installing the latest updates should get some more life out of your old Android phone. But updates will only take your phone so far, because newer updates are designed for newer phones with newer components. Old phone processors and less memory will have a hard time handling the demands of new OS versions, and that could cause performance lag. But a tradeoff in performance might be worth it if you want to get a little bit more life out of your older Android phone.

The obvious reality is, phones are not built to last forever, and you will need to replace your trusty old Android at some point. But following these tips could squeeze just a little bit more life out of your older Android phone so you can put off having to spend hundreds on a new one.

#281. Razer unveils the Raiju V3 Pro Signature Edition PS5 controller

It sure is pretty and will likely be expensive.

Razer just announced the Razer Raiju V3 Pro Signature Edition controller, a flagship gamepad made specifically for PS5 consoles. It looks absolutely gorgeous, with an open-shell design you can see into. See-through stuff is all the rage right now. There's also a big PlayStation button and a Razer logo up top.

It was built with premium materials. The black exoskeleton is made from magnesium alloy and there's a nano coating over the internals to keep out debris. Even the touchpad is semi-transparent, which is manufactured with laser-etched glass. The whole thing weighs just 260 grams, which is lighter than a standard DualSense controller. That's pretty cool.

Now let's move on to features. This is a pro-grade controller, so it can do a lot. It includes contactless TMR thumbsticks which should help with aiming precision. There are six mappable buttons, including two claw-grip bumpers and four mouse-click back buttons. These can be used to map hotkeys and the like. The buttons are made from durable polybutylene terephthalate, also called PBT. This is an extremely rigid and durable plastic.

It can be used with other devices, even though it has a big PlayStation logo. It looks especially useful for PC gamers, as it offers up to a 2,000Hz HyperPolling wireless rate. This means that it sends data to and from the PC 2,000 times every second.

The controller arrives in a collector's edition that includes a bunch of extra goodies. The package ships with a leatherette carrying case, alternate thumbstick caps, back button covers, a wireless dongle and tools for replacing parts.

The Razer Raiju V3 Pro Signature Edition will be available on November 10, but potential buyers had better not dilly-dally. The company says it's only making 1,337 of these things. That number might elicit a chuckle from some and a groan from others, as this is an old-school example of "leetspeak."

Razer hasn't released a price, but chances are it'll probably cost a pretty penny.
